extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical political philosophy; those studying Plato's Republic
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting Plato's evaluative criteria for virtues, justice, and the structure of soul/state from Republic Books IV–V; focuses on what counts as justice, temperance, courage, wisdom, and the proper education and ordering of parts. Useful for analysing moral/political theory and character/state evaluation in the dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance / self-mastery (harmonious rule of better over worse)
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the better has the worse under control, then a man is said to be master of himself... if the words 'temperance' and 'self-mastery' truly express the rule of the better part over the worse.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance is distinguished from courage and wisdom because it 'extends to the whole' and 'produces a harmony of the weaker and the stronger and the middle class.' It is an agreement between naturally superior and inferior about who ought to rule; appears in both rulers and subjects. Anti-pattern: the better being overwhelmed by the greater mass of the worse (then one is called slave of self and unprincipled).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice — doing one's own business / not being a busybody
rubrics_metrics.description: “We affirmed that justice was doing one’s own business, and not being a busybody.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the State, justice consists in each class performing its proper function (trader, auxiliary/warrior, guardian/ruler). In the individual, justice is realized when each part of the soul does its own work and does not interfere with the others. Verification method: if the state's and individual's structures agree, the conception is confirmed. Anti-pattern: meddling of one class with another or one part of soul doing another's work; termed the ruin of the State and injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice — legal/possession view (having and doing what is one's own)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Suits decided ... on the ground that a man may neither take what is another’s, nor be deprived of what is his own.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a judicial standpoint justice is having and doing what belongs to a man. This complements the 'doing one's own business' account: legal justice protects possessions and rights. Use this to judge whether a decision or law is just in terms of rightful possession and non-deprivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour / specialization as social justice criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: “One man should practise one thing only, the thing to which his nature was best adapted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-ordered city depends on each person performing the task for which nature fitted them. Harm arises when individuals attempt roles they are unsuited for (trader trying to be warrior, warrior trying to be legislator, or one person doing all roles). Thus evaluate institutions/people by fit of function to nature/skill; anti-pattern: interchange and meddling between classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite soul: rational, spirited, and appetitive principles
rubrics_metrics.description: “We may assume that [the individual] has the same three principles in his own soul which are found in the State... the rational principle... the irrational or appetitive... and passion or spirit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three principles to classify actions and dispositions: reason (seeks truth, rules), spirit (anger, honour — allied to reason when well-educated), appetitive (desires bodily pleasures, largest part). Examples: hunger and thirst are appetitive; spirit can side with reason against base desires. Diagnosis: conflicts among these parts indicate vice; harmony indicates virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage 'resides in a part only' and in the State is the quality that makes it valiant; in an individual 'he is to be deemed courageous whose spirit retains in pleasure and in pain the commands of reason about what he ought or ought not to fear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage is assessed by whether the spirited part (auxiliaries/soldiers) preserves the lawful opinion about dangers (the doctrine of the law about what is to be feared). It is not mere fearlessness but steadiness under pleasure and pain in accordance with reason's commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom is the quality of the rulers: knowledge and watchfulness about what is for the interest of each of the three parts and of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rulers (or governing principles) by their knowledge of the good for the whole and their prudence/watchfulness. Wisdom 'resides in a part only' (the ruling class) and contributes to the state's excellence when rulers are educated and capable of seeing the interest of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education by music and gymnastic to harmonize the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: “The united influence of music and gymnastic will bring them into accord, nerving and sustaining the reason with noble words and lessons, and moderating and soothing and civilizing the wildness of passion by harmony and rhythm.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an educational criterion, combine musical (culture, poetry, moral education) with physical training to align rational and spirited parts and keep the appetitive in check. Good education produces friendship among the parts so reason rules with willing consent; poor education allows appetites to dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as health and beauty of the soul; vice as disease
rubrics_metrics.description: “Virtue is the health and beauty and well-being of the soul, and vice the disease and weakness and deformity of the same.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral states by analogy to bodily health: justice/virtue produce an ordered, well-governed soul (health), while injustice/vice produce disorder (disease). Good practices cultivate virtue; bad practices produce vice. Practical test: just actions create justice; unjust actions create injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice as internal strife / meddlesomeness
rubrics_metrics.description: “Injustice ... a strife which arises among the three principles — a meddlesomeness, and interference, and rising up of a part of the soul against the whole ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of factional conflict among soul's parts (or social classes) as the diagnostic of injustice. Injustice correlates with intemperance, cowardice, ignorance, and other vices; it is the state produced when parts do not perform their proper roles and rebel against proper order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of city forms and soul forms (classification of regimes and souls)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are five of the State, and five of the soul... Such is the good and true City or State, and the good and true man is of the same pattern; and if this is right every other is wrong; and the evil is one which affects not only the ordering of the State, but also the regulation of the individual soul, and is exhibited in four forms.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate regimes (and souls) by their form: the well-ordered (monarchy/aristocracy) corresponds to the well-ordered soul; corrupt or degenerate states correspond to corrupted souls. The passage announces a typology to be applied: one 'good' form and several 'evil' forms, and the succession/order among them matters for moral diagnosis.
